# Febrile seizures

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Seizure disorders > Febrile seizures*

[Original Article Link](/library/D401lT)

---

## Summary

<u>Febrile</u> <u>seizures</u> affect children aged 6 months to 5 years and are associated with <u>fever</u> in the absence of <u>CNS</u> infection. They are one of the most common pediatric emergencies. <u>Simple febrile seizures</u> are <u>generalized seizures</u> that last < 15 minutes and do not recur within 24 hours. <u>Seizures</u> are classified as complex if they have a focal component, last longer than 15 minutes, or recur within 24 hours. Diagnostic examination focuses on addressing the cause of <u>fever</u>. Further diagnostics are required if there are any neurological abnormalities or signs of intracranial infection (e.g., <u>meningeal signs</u>) and may include <u>lumbar puncture</u> and <u>neuroimaging</u>. Most <u>febrile</u> <u>seizures</u> end spontaneously and do not require any treatment. Abortive therapy, typically with <u>benzodiazepines</u>, is indicated if a <u>seizure</u> lasts longer than five minutes. Most children with <u>simple febrile seizures</u> can be discharged. While the risk of recurrence is high, caregivers may be reassured that the overall prognosis of <u>febrile</u> <u>seizures</u> is good.




See “<u>Seizures and epilepsy</u>” for the management of other types of <u>seizures</u>.

---

## Definitions

<u>Seizures in children</u> aged 6 months to 5 years that are associated with <u>fever</u> (> 38Â°C (> 100.4Â°F)) in the absence of <u>CNS</u> infection, metabolic abnormalities, or a history of afebrile <u>seizures</u>. May be classified based on <u>clinical features of febrile seizures</u> into: [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)




* <u>Simple febrile seizures</u> (∼ 70% of all <u>febrile</u> <u>seizures</u>)

* <u>Complex febrile seizures</u> (∼ 25%)

* <u>Febrile status epilepticus</u> (∼ 5%)

---

## Etiology

The exact pathophysiological mechanisms of <u>febrile</u> <u>seizures</u> are not known. <u>Risk factors</u>:




* Genetic predisposition

* High <u>fever</u> (> 40Â°C (> 104Â°F))

* Viral infection (e.g., <u>HHV-6</u>, <u>influenza</u>)

* Recent <u>immunization</u> (especially <u>MMR vaccine</u> and <u>DTaP</u>)

---

## Clinical features

### Simple febrile seizure [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)[[2]](/library/UnWbsN0)




* Duration: < 15 minutes

* Frequency: : maximum of one <u>seizure</u> within 24 hours

* Features

* <u>Generalized seizures</u> (no focal component)

* Commonly <u>tonic-clonic</u>

* <u>Postictal phase</u>

* Quick return to normal

* Confusion and drowsiness may be present for < 30 minutes.





### Complex febrile seizure [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)[[2]](/library/UnWbsN0)




A <u>febrile</u> <u>seizure</u> is classified as complex if it meets any of the following criteria:




* Duration: ≥ 15 minutes or interrupted with abortive therapy

* Frequency: > 1 <u>seizure</u> within 24 hours

* Features: any <u>focal seizure</u>  [[2]](/library/UnWbsN0)

* <u>Postictal phase</u>: may include <u>focal neurological signs</u> and/or <u>postictal paralysis</u>





### Febrile status epilepticus [[2]](/library/UnWbsN0)[[3]](/library/2SdT_60)




* Any <u>febrile</u> <u>seizure</u> lasting > 30 minutes

* Any series of <u>febrile</u> <u>seizures</u> lasting > 30 minutes in total without full recovery of consciousness between <u>seizures</u>

* May be generalized or focal





> [!TIP]
> Prolonged drowsiness or new neurological abnormalities may be a sign of an underlying infectious disease (e.g., <u>meningitis</u>) or ongoing <u>seizure</u> activity. [[4]](/library/yhddgp0)

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[6]](/library/ThX6WB)




* Obtain a thorough history, including:

* Description of <u>seizure</u> activity

* Presence of a <u>postictal</u> period

* <u>Vaccination</u> history

* Perform a <u>physical examination</u> to evaluate for signs of:

* <u>Meningism</u>

* <u>Causes of pediatric fever</u>

* <u>Causes of seizures</u>

* Consider further diagnostics if there are <u>signs of meningitis</u> and/or abnormal neurological findings, e.g.:

* <u>Diagnostics for pediatric fever</u> as indicated to identify the cause of <u>fever</u>  [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)

* <u>BMP</u> and <u>POC blood glucose</u> if <u>altered mental status</u> persists between or after <u>seizures</u> [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)

* <u>Neuroimaging</u> and/or <u>lumbar puncture</u> if indicated

* For patients with <u>complex febrile seizures</u> or <u>febrile status epilepticus</u>, consult a pediatric and/or neurologic specialist for further diagnostics (e.g., <u>EEG</u>).





> [!TIP]
> <u>Simple febrile seizures</u> do not require a specific diagnostic workup. [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)




### <u>Neuroimaging</u> [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)[[2]](/library/UnWbsN0)[[7]](/library/Cgdqx60)




* Indications

* Abnormal <u>neurological examination</u>

* Focal <u>complex febrile seizures</u>  [[3]](/library/2SdT_60)

* Modalities

* <u>MRI</u> without IV contrast (preferred)

* CT without IV contrast (if <u>MRI</u> is unavailable)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Neuroimaging</u> is not indicated in the initial workup of <u>febrile</u> <u>seizures</u> if patients have returned to their baseline and do not have a neurological deficit. [[6]](/library/ThX6WB)[[7]](/library/Cgdqx60)




### <u>Lumbar puncture</u> [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)[[2]](/library/UnWbsN0)[[6]](/library/ThX6WB)




The main purpose is to exclude <u>CNS</u> infections, e.g., <u>bacterial meningitis</u>, <u>encephalitis</u>.




* Indications

* History or <u>physical examination</u> suggesting <u>CNS</u> infection (e.g., <u>meningeal signs</u>)

* <u>Febrile status epilepticus</u>

* Consider for children aged 6–12 months who are not vaccinated against <u>Haemophilus influenzae type b</u> or <u>Streptococcus pneumoniae</u>.

* Consider in children who have already received <u>antibiotics</u>.

* Contraindications: See “<u>Contraindications for lumbar puncture</u>.”

* Procedure: See “<u>Lumbar puncture</u>.”

---

## Treatment

### Approach [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)[[2]](/library/UnWbsN0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* <u>Simple febrile seizures</u> usually resolve spontaneously after a few minutes.

* Administer abortive therapy if a <u>seizure</u> lasts > 5 minutes. [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)

* Treat the underlying cause of <u>fever</u> (e.g., <u>antibiotics</u> for bacterial infections).

* Offer <u>supportive care for pediatric fever</u>, including <u>antipyretics</u>.  [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)[[9]](/library/WSdPA60)[[10]](/library/3hdSdp0)

* Reassure caregivers and educate them about the low risk of complications (see “Prognosis”).





### Abortive therapy [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)[[2]](/library/UnWbsN0)




* Indication: <u>seizure</u> activity lasting > 5 minutes (e.g., <u>febrile status epilepticus</u>)

* Agents

* Follow “<u>Phase-based acute seizure management</u>.”

* Preferred intravenous agents include <u>lorazepam</u> and <u>diazepam</u>.

* If <u>IV access</u> is unavailable, consider buccal <u>midazolam</u> or rectal <u>diazepam</u>.





### Disposition [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)[[2]](/library/UnWbsN0)[[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Most children who have returned to baseline can be discharged with close pediatric follow-up.

* Indications for admission include:

* Any child who has had a <u>lumbar puncture</u>

* Severely ill child

* Recurrent <u>seizures</u>

* Neurological abnormalities

* No return to baseline

* Unreliable follow-up

* Provide caregivers with:

* <u>Anticipatory guidance for pediatric fever</u>

* Information on the management of <u>seizure</u> recurrence, e.g.: [[2]](/library/UnWbsN0)[[11]](/library/XSd9y60)

* Protecting the child from injury by removing hazards

* Calling <u>EMS</u> for <u>seizures</u> lasting > 5 minutes





> [!TIP]
> Prophylaxis with <u>anticonvulsant drugs</u> is not usually indicated in patients with <u>simple febrile seizures</u>. [[9]](/library/WSdPA60)[[12]](/library/fhXkWB)

---

## Prognosis

Although <u>febrile</u> <u>seizures</u> are not typically associated with an increased risk of long-term neurological or cognitive impairment or increased mortality, there is an increased risk of recurrence and a minor risk of developing <u>epilepsy</u>. [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)[[13]](/library/Bgdzx60)




### Risk of recurrence [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)[[12]](/library/fhXkWB)




* Risk depends on the child's age at onset.

* Approx. 30% in children > 12 months

* Approx. 50% in children < 12 months

* <u>Risk factors</u> for recurrence

* Age < 18 months at onset

* <u>Febrile</u> <u>seizure</u> less than 1 hour after onset of <u>fever</u>

* <u>Febrile</u> <u>seizures</u> in <u>first-degree relatives</u>

* <u>Febrile</u> <u>seizure</u> at < 40.0Â°C (< 104Â°F)





> [!TIP]
> More than one-third of all children with a <u>febrile</u> <u>seizure</u> will experience at least one other <u>febrile</u> <u>seizure</u>. [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)




### Risk of developing <u>epilepsy</u> [[2]](/library/UnWbsN0)[[12]](/library/fhXkWB)




* Approx. 1% in children with a single <u>simple febrile seizure</u>  [[12]](/library/fhXkWB)

* 2–3% in children with multiple <u>simple febrile seizures</u>, onset at < 12 months of age, and <u>family history</u> of <u>epilepsy</u> [[12]](/library/fhXkWB)

* 6–8% overall in children with <u>complex febrile seizures</u>  [[2]](/library/UnWbsN0)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Simple febrile seizures</u> are not associated with an increased risk of neurocognitive or behavioral abnormalities. [[1]](/library/g1WFT40)
